claims.text: The initial alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is in the cast state.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
HfNbTaTiZr has inadequate oxidation resistance for high-temperature use in air.
A thin, adherent alumina coating can be deposited on HfNbTaTiZr by chemical vapor deposition.
Applying an alumina coating will significantly improve the alloy's resistance to oxygen attack during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The alumina coating will not degrade the alloy's intrinsic mechanical performance.
The intervention produces a continuous, dense alumina layer.
A continuous, dense alumina layer acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress.
The alumina coating prevents oxygen diffusion into the underlying HfNbTaTiZr.
Preventing oxygen diffusion minimizes oxide-scale formation.
Limiting oxygen ingress preserves the alloy's microstructure and mechanical properties during high-temperature exposure.
After 100 hours in air at 1000 °C, coated specimens will have less oxide-scale formation and mass gain than uncoated specimens.
After treatment and exposure, the coated alloy will retain 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
After treatment and exposure, the coated alloy will retain a high-temperature yield strength of 163–530 MPa.
Oxygen exposure degrades the performance of untreated HfNbTaTiZr at high temperature.
Thermal cycling and thermal-expansion mismatch between alumina and HfNbTaTiZr may reduce coating durability.

contradictions.description: The conditions and boundary describe high-temperature exposure under mechanical loading, whereas the falsification experiment exposes specimens first and only subsequently performs tensile testing. The experiment therefore does not test coating integrity during simultaneous 100-hour oxidation and mechanical loading.
